comparison: Perfect agreement on genetic evidence (C3, C28, C29, C33). Both evaluations find the DNAH12 variants are pathogenic and well-supported by segregation analysis, rarity, and computational predictions. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Perfect agreement on clinical phenotype characterization (C34-C37). Both evaluations accept the sperm morphological abnormalities and molecular evidence of protein loss as well-supported by multiple complementary methods.

Strong agreement on ultrastructural findings (C38-C42, with peer also noting C4). Both evaluations find the TEM and immunofluorescence data demonstrating specific loss of IDA and CP components to be well-supported and internally consistent.

Agreement on mouse model findings (C43-C48, with peer also noting C5) but peer reviewers note phenotypic severity differences between mice and patients that were 'not fully explained.' OpenEval finds the model well-supported; peer reviewers accept findings after author response but acknowledge discrepancy.

Perfect agreement on mouse sperm axonemal protein localization (C52-C54). Both evaluations find the TEM, immunoblotting, and immunofluorescence data showing specific loss of IDA and CP components to be strongly supported.

Perfect agreement on ICSI rescue experiments (C10, C77, C104). Both evaluations accept the findings that ICSI can overcome the infertility phenotype, demonstrating the defect is primarily motility-related.

Partial agreement on DNAH12-DNALI1-DNAH1 interactions (C7, C60, C61, C63). OpenEval finds Co-IP and mass spec data well-supported. Peer reviewers accept experimental data but express concern that computational structural predictions (C62) require further validation.

Strong agreement on IDA recruitment defects (C8, C64-C66, with peer also noting C78). Both evaluations find the temporal analysis showing normal early expression but failed recruitment to be well-supported and mechanistically informative.

Partial agreement on RS protein interactions (C9, C71, C73-C76). OpenEval finds the mass spec, Co-IP, and AlphaFold3 modeling supportive. Peer reviewers accept Co-IP data but express concern that computational predictions require further validation, similar to their concern about DNALI1/DNAH1 structural modeling.

Strong agreement on spermiogenesis defects (C49-C51, with peer also noting C92). Both evaluations accept the immunofluorescence, TEM, and TUNEL data showing temporal progression of defects and manchette abnormalities.

Strong agreement on DNAH12 expression patterns (C30-C32, with peer also noting C89). Both evaluations accept the RT-PCR, qPCR, immunoblotting, and phylogenetic data as part of comprehensive characterization.

Strong agreement on hierarchical IDA assembly (C69-C70, with peer also noting C79). Both evaluations accept the mutual dependence of DNAH12, DNALI1, and DNAH1 for proper localization, though OpenEval notes reliance on single patient family.

Agreement on tissue-specific effects (C6, C55-C56 from OpenEval; C6, C55-C56, C67-C68, C98 from peer). Both evaluations accept the differential effects in flagella versus cilia as a key finding, with peer reviewers noting this provides 'a unique perspective.'

Agreement on respiratory cilia findings (C67-C68, C98). Both evaluations accept that DNAH12 loss does not affect respiratory cilia IDA/CP assembly, explaining lack of PCD symptoms. Peer review groups this with broader tissue-specific findings.

Agreement on DNAH12 interactome findings (C58-C59, with peer also noting C57). Both evaluations accept the mass spectrometry and GO analysis data. OpenEval notes validation focused on specific candidates; peer reviewers accept the biochemical approaches as a strength.

Agreement on comparative phenotype analysis (C82-C86). Both evaluations accept the comparison with other dynein deficiencies showing DNAH12 has milder phenotype. Peer reviewers note phenotypic differences were addressed satisfactorily by authors.
Agreement on DNAH12 structural features (C2, C24, C57). Both evaluations accept that DNAH12 lacks MTBD and requires interaction partners. Peer review groups this with broader interactome findings.

Divergent evaluation of computational predictions (C62, C74). OpenEval finds AlphaFold3 predictions supportive though notes experimental validation is stronger for DNALI1 than RS proteins. Peer reviewers explicitly state computational models 'require further validation' and rate as UNCERTAIN.

Similar to R17-R6 pairing: OpenEval finds computational docking (C62, C74) supportive with caveats about validation. Peer reviewers express concern that in silico methodologies require further validation.

Agreement on comparative sperm count analysis (C82). Both evaluations accept the comparison suggesting DNAH12 may have additional functions beyond recruiting DNALI1/DNAH1, though OpenEval notes direct comparison would be more rigorous.

Agreement on manchette and developmental defects (C89, C92-C93). Both evaluations accept the temporal and spatial localization patterns, though OpenEval notes mechanistic connection could be more direct.
Agreement on DNAH12 localization during spermiogenesis (C89). Both evaluations accept the expression and localization findings as part of comprehensive characterization.

OpenEval evaluates clinical absence of PCD symptoms (C96-C97) as supported by clinical history. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though peer reviewers accept tissue-specific findings broadly.

OpenEval evaluates background claims about male infertility prevalence and genetics (C1, C12-C14) as supported by established literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation as these are contextual background claims.

OpenEval evaluates background claims about genetic heterogeneity of asthenoteratozoospermia (C15-C16, C21-C23) as supported by citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation as these are contextual background claims.

OpenEval evaluates background claims about axoneme structure and dynein function (C17-C20) as supported by established literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation as these are contextual background claims.
OpenEval evaluates background claims about DNAH12 knowledge gaps (C25-C26, C101) as supported by citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation as these establish study rationale.
OpenEval evaluates background claims about ICSI clinical context (C102-C103) as supported by multiple studies. No corresponding peer review evaluation as these are contextual background claims.

OpenEval evaluates claims about coordinated manchette and axoneme assembly (C90-C91, C94-C95) as supported but somewhat speculative. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation, though peer reviewers accept developmental findings broadly.

Agreement on main mechanistic conclusions (C11, C78-C81). OpenEval finds these well-supported by collective evidence with appropriate qualifications. Peer reviewers accept the mechanistic findings about DNAH12's role in recruiting axonemal proteins.

Partial overlap on assembly hierarchy conclusions (C79). OpenEval groups this with main conclusions; peer reviewers accept hierarchical assembly findings as providing insight into spermatogenesis mechanisms.
OpenEval evaluates study cohort description (C27) as adequately documented. No corresponding peer review evaluation as this is a methodological detail.
